title: Obadiah 1:1–9
context: The book is introduced as the vision of Obadiah, and the Lord GOD speaks about Edom, the people descended from Esau (Genesis 36:8). Nothing is known of the prophet beyond his name. The date and occasion are uncertain: many interpreters connect the book with Edom’s conduct when Jerusalem fell to Babylon, commonly dated to 586 BC (compare Psalm 137:7), while others propose an earlier setting, such as Edom’s revolt against Judah in the ninth century (2 Kings 8:20). The prophet reports news from the LORD that an envoy has gone among the nations to rise against Edom. The LORD says he has made Edom small; its proud heart has deceived it, dwelling in the clefts of the rock and nesting high like an eagle, but he will bring it down. Thieves and grape pickers would leave something behind, but Esau will be ransacked; allies will betray Edom, and the LORD will destroy its wise men and dismay the warriors of Teman, commonly understood as a region or town in Edom. Verses 1–9 closely parallel Jeremiah 49:7–22, especially Jeremiah 49:14–16 (compare verses 1–4), 49:9–10 (compare verses 5–6), and 49:7 (compare verse 8); interpreters discuss the relationship between the two texts without agreement on which came first. Compare also Amos 1:11–12, Ezekiel 25:12–14, and Ezekiel 35. Shared ground: Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the passage as a warning that God humbles pride and rules over the nations.

verses.text: The vision of Obadiah. This is what the Lord GOD says about Edom. We have heard news from the LORD, and an ambassador is sent among the nations, saying, “Arise, and let’s rise up against her in battle.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the vision of Obadiah, with the Lord GOD speaking about Edom and an envoy rousing the nations. God stirs the nations to carry out his word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign word about a neighboring nation. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the opening as a reminder that the LORD governs the nations (compare Jeremiah 49:14).

verses.text: Behold, I have made you small among the nations. You are greatly despised.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he has made Edom small among the nations and greatly despised. A proud people is humbled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s power to raise up and bring down nations. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as showing that human greatness depends on God (compare Jeremiah 49:15).

verses.text: The pride of your heart has deceived you, you who dwell in the clefts of the rock, whose habitation is high, who says in his heart, ‘Who will bring me down to the ground?’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Edom deceived by the pride of its heart, trusting its high rocky dwelling and asking who could bring it down. Pride blinds.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the self-deception of pride, which imagines itself beyond reach (compare Isaiah 14:13). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as a warning that pride goes before a fall (Proverbs 16:18).

verses.text: Though you mount on high as the eagle, and though your nest is set among the stars, I will bring you down from there,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying that even if Edom nests among the stars, he will bring it down. No height is beyond God’s reach.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty over the proud (compare James 4:6). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as a clear statement that God humbles those who exalt themselves.

verses.text: “If thieves came to you, if robbers by night—oh, what disaster awaits you—wouldn’t they only steal until they had enough? If grape pickers came to you, wouldn’t they leave some gleaning grapes?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the image of thieves and grape pickers, who would leave something behind. Edom’s loss will be more complete than ordinary theft.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the thoroughness of the coming judgment (compare Jeremiah 49:9). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse soberly, as a picture of total loss.

verses.text: How Esau will be ransacked! How his hidden treasures are sought out!
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Esau ransacked and his hidden treasures sought out. What Edom hid away in its rocky strongholds will be exposed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see nothing hidden from God (compare Jeremiah 49:10). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as a warning that wealth stored in pride offers no security.

verses.text: All the men of your alliance have brought you on your way, even to the border. The men who were at peace with you have deceived you, and prevailed against you. Friends who eat your bread lay a snare under you. There is no understanding in him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Edom’s allies deceiving it, pushing it to the border, and setting a snare, while those who ate its bread betray it. Trust in alliances fails.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see betrayal by friends as part of Edom’s judgment (compare Psalm 41:9). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as showing the emptiness of trusting human alliances over God.

verses.text: “Won’t I in that day”, says the LORD, “destroy the wise men out of Edom, and understanding out of the mountain of Esau?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether he will not destroy the wise men of Edom in that day. Edom’s famed wisdom cannot save it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see human wisdom brought to nothing before God (compare Jeremiah 49:7). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as humbling human cleverness.

verses.text: Your mighty men, Teman, will be dismayed, to the end that everyone may be cut off from the mountain of Esau by slaughter.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the warriors of Teman dismayed and the mountain of Esau cut off. Military strength fails before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s judgment reaching Edom’s defenders. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse soberly, holding the identification of Teman with appropriate care.
